correctness.rationale: At fixed latent p the probability of a red terminal draw is p, giving the beta posterior with first parameter increased by one. One common sequence of iid nonterminal bits given P produces the stated coupling. For 2≤i≤n, direct Laplacian multiplication on the vector with coordinates 1 before i, −(i−1) at i and zero later gives eigenvalue iZ_i plus the later red count. The forced last draw gives eigenvalue n and cancels the matrix-tree cofactor factor 1/n. At i<n the deterministic baseline is at least p(n−i), the later centered count is independent of Z_i, and there is an additional bounded terminal correction. Cutting at k=n−i≥ceil(n^{1/3}), the simultaneous Hoeffding bound O(sqrt(k log n)+1) has summable failure probability. Summing the Taylor remainder gives O(log² n); the omitted logs are bounded in total by O(n^{1/3} log n), since eigenvalues are between 1 and n. Replacing the random reciprocal by its mean produces orthogonal reverse martingale differences with total variance O(sum 1/k)=O(log n). The terminal correction in the remaining linear term is O(log n). The cumulative reciprocal coefficients approximate their integral uniformly to O(1/ceil(n^{1/3})) off the last block, and the tail coefficient errors are O(log n) each, giving o(n) total squared error. Adding the direct bit coefficient to this cumulative integral gives the claimed g_p; its integrable logarithmic-square singularity gives convergence of normalized squared sums, while its maximal coefficient is o(sqrt(n)). This establishes Lindeberg's condition and the variance formula. The deterministic centering integral gives f(p); the Taylor correction is o(n) almost surely, and weighted Hoeffding on the retained direct bits gives the strong law. Integrating conditional bounded test expectations establishes stability relative to P; on the given coupling, removal of any fixed finite set of bits from the weighted sum also gives stable convergence against fixed finite-bit tests and then their bounded measurable limits. At p=1/2 the substitution y=tanh(u) evaluates the variance to π²/3. The weight is positive for 0<y<1; v(p) tends to zero at p→1 and is at least 2(1−p)/p near zero, so the full-support beta mixture is genuinely nondegenerate in variance. Strict monotonicity of f follows from −log p≥1−p and differentiation, with the stated endpoint limits.
residual_risks: All expansion constants are fixed-p; the proof and verdict do not assert a uniform endpoint rate or finite annealed variance. Stable mixing of bounded tests does not require the latter.

evidence: Yu et al. give the beta-binomial model and Laplacian spectrum. Diaconis–Holmes–Janson treat the same iid creation model before terminal conditioning; their degree law converges to density (1−p)/p on (0,p) and p/(1−p) on (p,1), and §9 relates normalized spectral and degree weak limits.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Integrating log against the known limiting density gives the frozen centering function, but weak convergence alone does not justify that operation on finite spectra, much less its fluctuations at rate sqrt(n). The inspected spectrum results do not give the direct-bit and accumulated tail contributions to the variance.

value.rationale: The logarithm of the tree count is a natural measure of graph complexity, and one cannot infer its fluctuations from the normalized spectrum or latent-proportion law alone. The result separates order-n environmental variation from order-sqrt(n) conditional variation and supplies the nonconstant variance that determines the mixture. It also handles the logarithmic sensitivity to small eigenvalues near the terminal end instead of replacing the observable by a bounded spectral statistic.
residual_risks: The result is specific to positive fixed urn parameters and terminal-red-conditioned ordinary spanning trees. No general random graph or endpoint-uniform theorem follows.
